title: The Georgia Foreclosure Timeline: How Little Time You Actually Have
desc: Georgia foreclosures are non-judicial and can finish in about 60 days. There's no redemption after the sale. Here's the real timeline and where your exits are.
answer: Georgia foreclosure moves faster than almost anywhere else. It's non-judicial, so no judge is involved, and from first missed payment to a completed courthouse-steps auction can run as little as 60 days. Sales happen on the first Tuesday of the month. Critically, there is no right of redemption after a non-judicial foreclosure sale in Georgia — once the gavel falls, the house is gone. The 12-month redemption people hear about applies to tax sales and to judicial foreclosures, which are rare here.

p: Most states make a lender either sue you or wait. Georgia does neither. Your security deed almost certainly contains a power of sale clause, and that clause lets the lender sell the property without ever filing a lawsuit.
The practical effect is speed. A Florida homeowner in default might have a year. A Georgia homeowner might have two months.
It runs in a predictable order, and knowing where you are tells you what's still possible.
list: Day 1–30. You miss a payment. Late fee posts. Servicer starts calling.
Day 30–90. The delinquency gets reported to credit bureaus. The servicer's loss mitigation department may reach out about forbearance or modification. This is the cheapest place to fix it.
Day 120. Federal servicing rules generally bar the first foreclosure filing until you're more than 120 days delinquent. This is a floor, not a guarantee.
Notice of sale. Georgia requires the lender to send written notice to the borrower and to publish the sale in the county's legal organ newspaper once a week for four weeks before the sale.
First Tuesday. The sale happens on the courthouse steps of the county where the property sits, between 10am and 4pm.

p: This is the part that catches people. In Georgia, after a non-judicial foreclosure sale, you have no statutory right to buy the house back.
sections.callout: If someone tells you that you have twelve months to redeem your home after a Georgia foreclosure, they're describing either a tax sale (which does carry a 12-month redemption) or a judicial foreclosure (which almost never happens here). Don't plan around a right you don't have.

sections.h: What you can still do before the sale date
p: Right up until the auction is completed, the property is yours to sell. A sale pays the loan off, the foreclosure gets cancelled, and anything above the payoff is yours.
list: Reinstate. Pay the arrears plus fees and the loan goes current. Ask the servicer for a written reinstatement quote good through a specific date.
Loan modification or forbearance. If your income can support a restructured payment, this keeps you in the house. Call loss mitigation, not collections.
Sell. A conventional listing takes 30–60 days after you get an accepted offer, which is often too slow this late. A cash sale can close in 7.
Short sale. If you owe more than it's worth, this needs lender approval and typically runs 45–90 days. Start early or don't start.

p: If the property sells at auction for more than the debt, the excess belongs to you. Recovering it means filing a claim, and in practice it's slow and frequently contested by junior lienholders. Selling before the sale puts that same money in your hands at closing instead.

faqs.q: How fast can a foreclosure happen in Georgia?
faqs.a: As little as about 60 days from the first missed payment to a completed sale, because Georgia is non-judicial and no court has to approve anything. Federal rules generally prevent the first filing before you're 120 days delinquent, but once it starts it moves quickly.

faqs.q: Do I have a right of redemption after foreclosure in Georgia?
faqs.a: Not after a non-judicial foreclosure sale, which is what almost every Georgia foreclosure is. A 12-month statutory redemption exists only for judicial foreclosures. Georgia tax sales are separate and do carry a 12-month redemption from the sale date.

faqs.q: When are foreclosure sales held in Georgia?
faqs.a: On the first Tuesday of the month, on the courthouse steps of the county where the property is located, generally between 10am and 4pm.

faqs.q: Can I sell my house after the foreclosure has been advertised?
faqs.a: Yes. Until the sale is actually completed, you still own the property and can sell it. The payoff comes out of the closing proceeds and the foreclosure is cancelled. What you can't do is sell after the auction.

faqs.q: What is the legal organ newspaper?
faqs.a: It's the newspaper a Georgia county designates for official legal notices. Foreclosure sales must be advertised there once a week for four weeks before the sale date, which is also how you can verify a sale is actually scheduled.

title: Florida Foreclosure Timeline: Why You Have Longer Than You Think, and Less Than You Need
desc: Florida foreclosure is judicial and typically takes 8 months to 2 years. But there's no redemption after the sale. Here's the sequence and where the exits are.
answer: Florida is a judicial foreclosure state. The lender has to file a lawsuit in circuit court and get a judge's order before anything is sold, which is why the process typically takes 8 months to 2 years — roughly 6 to 12 months for an uncontested case, 18 to 36 months if you fight it. The tradeoff: Florida gives no post-sale right of redemption. Your right to redeem ends when the certificate of sale is filed.

sections.h: The lawsuit is the whole difference
p: In Georgia a lender can sell your house without asking anyone. In Florida it has to sue you, serve you, prove it owns the note, and get a judgment. Every one of those steps takes time, and every one is a place where you can respond.

That's why Florida timelines are measured in quarters, not weeks. Court dockets in Miami-Dade, Broward, Hillsborough, and Duval carry heavy foreclosure volume, and that backlog works in a homeowner's favor.

list: Default and notice. The servicer sends a breach letter giving you a window, commonly 30 days, to cure.
Lis pendens and complaint. The lender files suit in the circuit court for the county where the property sits and records a lis pendens. You're served.
20 days to respond. This matters. Not answering means a default judgment and a much faster path to sale.
Summary judgment or trial. Most uncontested cases end at summary judgment.
Judgment sets the sale date. The court schedules the sale, typically 30 to 120 days out. Statute requires at least 20 days' notice.
Auction. Most Florida counties run these online through the clerk's site.
Certificate of Sale, then 10 days, then Certificate of Title. Objections can be filed in that 10-day window. When title issues, ownership transfers.

p: Florida's redemption right exists only up to the moment the certificate of sale is filed. After that, it's over.
sections.callout: The long timeline lulls people. A homeowner who's been in litigation for 14 months can start to feel like the case will never end — and then the judgment lands and the sale is 45 days out. Treat the judgment, not the complaint, as the real alarm.

sections.h: Hurricane damage and insurance complicate this
p: A lot of Florida defaults trace back to a storm: the settlement didn't cover the repair, the house sat damaged, and the payments slipped. If your lender is a payee on the insurance check, that money may be sitting in escrow controlled by the servicer, and it's worth asking loss mitigation directly what's there.
Selling a storm-damaged house before a judgment is usually the cleanest exit, because a cash buyer doesn't need the repairs finished and doesn't need the insurance claim resolved first.

Florida allows them. If the sale doesn't cover the debt, the lender can pursue you for the shortfall, subject to a statutory limit tied to the property's fair market value. That's another argument for selling rather than letting it run.

faqs.q: How long does foreclosure take in Florida?
faqs.a: Typically 8 months to 2 years. Uncontested cases commonly resolve in 6 to 12 months from filing. Contested ones stretch to 18 to 36 months or longer depending on the county's docket.

faqs.q: Can I get my house back after a Florida foreclosure sale?
faqs.a: No. Florida provides no post-sale statutory right of redemption. Your right to redeem ends when the certificate of sale is filed, so the sale date is the deadline that matters.

faqs.q: What happens between the auction and losing the house?
faqs.a: The winning bidder gets a Certificate of Sale. A 10-day objection period runs. If no valid objection is filed, the clerk issues a Certificate of Title and ownership transfers.

faqs.q: Should I respond to the foreclosure complaint?
faqs.a: Yes. You generally have 20 days after service to file a response. Not responding leads to a default judgment, which removes most of the time advantage Florida's judicial process gives you. Talk to a Florida foreclosure attorney.

faqs.q: Can I sell my Florida house while the foreclosure case is pending?
faqs.a: Yes, at any point before the certificate of sale issues. The payoff is satisfied from closing proceeds and the case gets dismissed. Because Florida timelines are long, sellers here often have more room to work with than in Georgia or Tennessee.

title: Alabama's Right of Redemption: One Year, or 180 Days, and Why It Rarely Helps
desc: Alabama is one of the few states giving homeowners a redemption right after the foreclosure sale. Here's how it works, when it shrinks to 180 days, and its practical limits.
answer: Alabama gives homeowners a redemption right after the foreclosure sale, which most Southeastern states do not. The general period is one year. It drops to 180 days when three things are all true: the loan originated on or after January 1, 2016, a homestead exemption was claimed for the tax year in which the sale occurred, and the lender gave the required redemption notice at least 30 days before the sale. Redeeming means paying the full sale price plus statutory charges, which is why few owners actually use it.

p: The right sounds like a safety net, and legally it is one. Practically, it's a purchase option at a price most people in foreclosure can't pay.

To redeem you generally have to pay the foreclosure sale price, plus interest at the statutory rate, plus taxes the purchaser paid, plus insurance, plus the value of permanent improvements the purchaser made. That last item is the one that surprises people: an investor who renovates the house during your redemption period can add that cost to your redemption price.
The shortened period applies to most modern owner-occupied loans, which means the majority of Alabama homeowners foreclosed on today have six months, not twelve.
sections.callout: Check three things: when your loan originated, whether you claimed a homestead exemption for the tax year of the sale, and whether the lender sent a redemption notice at least 30 days before the sale. If all three line up, your window is 180 days.

p: Alabama permits both judicial and non-judicial foreclosure, and lenders take the non-judicial route almost every time because it's faster. The power of sale clause in your mortgage authorizes it, notice gets published in a county newspaper, and the sale happens at the courthouse door.

sections.h: Why selling first usually nets more
p: Compare two paths. In the first, the house goes to auction, sells below market to a bidder, and you're left with a redemption right you can't fund and possibly a deficiency. In the second, you sell before the sale, the payoff is satisfied at closing, and you keep whatever equity is left.
The second path is worth more in almost every case where equity exists. The redemption right is a backstop for a narrow set of situations, mostly where an owner comes into money after the fact.
Alabama allows the lender to pursue a deficiency when the sale doesn't cover the debt. That liability survives the foreclosure and can be collected against you afterward.

faqs.q: How long is the right of redemption in Alabama?
faqs.a: Generally one year after the foreclosure sale. It's 180 days if the loan originated on or after January 1, 2016, a homestead exemption was claimed for the tax year of the sale, and the lender gave proper redemption notice at least 30 days before the sale.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to redeem a house in Alabama?
faqs.a: Generally the foreclosure sale price plus statutory interest, taxes and insurance the purchaser paid, and the value of permanent improvements they made. That last component can grow substantially if the buyer renovates during your redemption window.

faqs.q: Is Alabama a judicial or non-judicial foreclosure state?
faqs.a: Both are permitted, but lenders almost always use non-judicial foreclosure under the power of sale clause because it's faster and doesn't require a lawsuit.

faqs.q: Can the lender come after me for the difference?
faqs.a: Yes. Alabama allows deficiency judgments when the foreclosure sale proceeds don't cover the debt owed.

faqs.q: Is it better to sell before the sale or rely on redemption?
faqs.a: Selling first is almost always better when you have equity. Redemption requires paying the full sale price plus charges in a lump sum, which is out of reach for most owners who were already behind on payments.

title: North Carolina's 10-Day Upset Bid: Why a Foreclosure Sale Isn't Final on Sale Day
desc: NC foreclosures need a clerk's hearing first, and after the sale a 10-day upset bid window runs — restarting with every new bid. Here's what that means for you.
answer: North Carolina sits between judicial and non-judicial foreclosure. A power of sale foreclosure can't proceed until the Clerk of Superior Court in the property's county holds a hearing and authorizes it. After the sale there's a 10-day upset bid period, and every new upset bid starts a fresh 10-day clock. The procedure lives in Chapter 45, Article 2A of the General Statutes. There is no post-sale redemption right.

sections.h: The clerk's hearing is a real checkpoint
p: Unlike Georgia or Tennessee, where a trustee can simply sell, North Carolina requires a hearing before the Clerk of Superior Court. The clerk has to find four things: a valid debt, a default, the lender's right to foreclose under the instrument, and proper notice to the borrower.

You're entitled to appear. Many homeowners don't, and that's a missed opportunity — not because clerks routinely deny these, but because the hearing is a scheduled, public date that anchors the timeline.

After the sale, the high bid sits open for 10 days. Anyone can raise it by the statutory increment and become the new high bidder — which starts another 10-day period. In an active market a property can bounce through several rounds.
sections.callout: The practical consequence: a North Carolina foreclosure sale is not final on sale day. The timeline can extend well past what the auction date suggests, and the final price is often higher than the opening bid.

p: Once the upset bid period finally runs without a new bid, the sale is confirmed and it's over. North Carolina gives no post-sale statutory redemption period, so the confirmation is the hard line.

North Carolina requires an attorney to handle the title work and the closing. If you're selling to avoid a foreclosure, the attorney's calendar becomes part of your timeline, so engage one early rather than assuming a closing can be squeezed in.

Up until the sale is confirmed, you own the property and can sell it. Because the clerk's hearing gives you a fixed, known date, North Carolina is one of the easier states to plan a pre-foreclosure sale around. A cash sale closing in 7 to 28 days fits comfortably inside most NC timelines if you start when the hearing is noticed rather than after the sale.

faqs.q: What is an upset bid in North Carolina?
faqs.a: After a foreclosure sale, a 10-day period runs during which anyone can submit a higher bid and become the new high bidder. Each new upset bid restarts a fresh 10-day period, so the process can extend well past the original sale date.

faqs.q: Do I have a right of redemption after foreclosure in North Carolina?
faqs.a: No. Once the upset bid period expires without a new bid and the sale is confirmed, the sale is final. What you have instead of redemption is the upset bid window itself.

faqs.q: What happens at the clerk's foreclosure hearing?
faqs.a: The Clerk of Superior Court determines whether there's a valid debt, a default, the right to foreclose under the deed of trust, and proper notice to the borrower. A power of sale foreclosure can't proceed without this authorization.

faqs.q: Can I still sell my house before the sale is confirmed?
faqs.a: Yes. Until confirmation you own the property. The mortgage payoff comes out of closing proceeds and the foreclosure is resolved.

faqs.q: Do I need an attorney to sell my house in North Carolina?
faqs.a: North Carolina requires an attorney to handle the title work and closing on a real estate transaction. Build their availability into your timeline.

title: Tennessee Trustee Sales: Fast, and That Two-Year Redemption Probably Doesn't Apply to You
desc: Tennessee foreclosures are non-judicial trustee sales. The two-year redemption right you'll read about is waived in most deeds of trust. Here's what's actually true.
answer: Tennessee uses non-judicial trustee sales. A trustee acting for the lender sells the property under the power of sale clause in your deed of trust, with no lawsuit and no judge. Tennessee law does provide a two-year right of redemption — but only if that right wasn't waived in the original deed of trust, and most Tennessee deeds of trust waive it. Check your document before relying on it. Deficiency judgments are allowed.

p: This is the single most important thing on this page. The two-year redemption right that comes up in every search result is a default rule that can be contracted away, and lenders contract it away as a matter of routine.

Pull your closing packet and look for language waiving the equity of redemption or the statutory right of redemption. If it's there — and it usually is — you have no redemption period at all, and the sale date is absolute.

Without a court, the timeline is driven by notice requirements. Once the trustee publishes notice and the statutory period runs, the sale happens. Tennessee is among the faster foreclosure states in the Southeast, closer to Georgia than to Florida.
sections.callout: If you're in default in Memphis, Nashville, Knoxville, or Chattanooga and you've received a notice of trustee's sale, treat the sale date as final. Don't plan around redemption unless you've confirmed in writing that your deed of trust preserved it.

p: Tennessee permits the lender to pursue you for the shortfall between the sale price and the debt. A trustee sale at a depressed price can leave a real balance, and that balance is collectible after you've already lost the house.
Selling before the sale, at a price that satisfies the payoff, eliminates that exposure entirely.

Shelby County has one of the largest single-family rental inventories in the country, and a large share of Tennessee's distressed sales are landlords rather than owner-occupants. If you're a tired landlord with a non-paying tenant and a mounting payoff, you can sell the property occupied. You don't have to evict first.

faqs.q: Does Tennessee have a right of redemption after foreclosure?
faqs.a: Statutory law provides a two-year redemption period, but it can be and usually is waived in the deed of trust. Check your closing documents. If the waiver is there, you have no redemption right and the sale is final.

faqs.q: Is Tennessee a judicial foreclosure state?
faqs.a: No. Tennessee uses non-judicial trustee sales under the power of sale clause in a deed of trust. No lawsuit is required, which makes the process comparatively fast.

faqs.q: Can the lender sue me after a Tennessee foreclosure?
faqs.a: Yes. Deficiency judgments are permitted, so if the sale doesn't cover the debt the lender can pursue you for the difference.

faqs.q: How fast can a Tennessee foreclosure happen?
faqs.a: Because there's no court involvement, the timeline is driven by the statutory notice and publication requirements rather than a docket. It's among the faster processes in the Southeast.

faqs.q: Can I sell a rental in Memphis with a tenant still in it?
faqs.a: Yes. The lease transfers with the property and a cash buyer takes over as landlord at closing. No eviction is required before the sale, and no showings are needed.

title: South Carolina Foreclosure: The Master-in-Equity, the 30-Day Upset Bid, and No Redemption
desc: SC foreclosures go through court, usually before a Master-in-Equity. There's no redemption after the sale — only a 30-day upset bid window, and only sometimes.
answer: South Carolina is a judicial foreclosure state. The lender files suit and the case is usually heard by a Master-in-Equity rather than a jury. There is no statutory right of redemption after the sale. What exists instead is the upset bid window: if the lender preserved its right to a deficiency judgment, bidding stays open until the 30th day after the sale. Many lenders waive the deficiency specifically to avoid that delay, which closes the window faster than owners expect.

sections.h: The deficiency decision drives your timeline
p: This is the quirk worth understanding. Whether you get a 30-day upset bid period depends entirely on a choice the lender makes for its own reasons.

If the lender wants the right to chase you for a shortfall, it must leave bidding open for 30 days after the sale. If it waives the deficiency, the sale closes faster. So a lender's decision to let you off the hook financially is also the decision that shortens your remaining time.

Most South Carolina counties refer foreclosures to a Master-in-Equity, a judicial officer who handles equity cases. Charleston, Beaufort, Richland, Greenville, and Horry counties all do. The Master hears the case, enters judgment, and orders the sale.
South Carolina requires a licensed South Carolina attorney to supervise the real estate closing. That's a firm requirement, not a custom, and it affects how quickly a sale can be scheduled.
sections.callout: If you're selling to get ahead of a foreclosure in Beaufort, Bluffton, Charleston, or Myrtle Beach, contact a closing attorney at the same time you contact a buyer. Their calendar is often the binding constraint, not the buyer's.

p: Beaufort and Jasper counties sit directly across the river from Savannah, and a lot of the housing stock there is exposed to flood zones and rising insurance costs. Premium increases have pushed owners into default who were never behind on the mortgage itself.
If insurance is what broke the budget rather than the loan, say so early. It changes what options actually help.

faqs.q: Is South Carolina a judicial foreclosure state?
faqs.a: Yes. The lender must file a lawsuit, and the case is typically heard by a Master-in-Equity rather than a jury.

faqs.q: Do I have a right of redemption in South Carolina?
faqs.a: No statutory right of redemption after the sale. The only post-sale mechanism is the upset bid period, and that only runs when the lender has preserved its right to a deficiency judgment.

faqs.q: How long is the upset bid period in South Carolina?
faqs.a: Bidding stays open until the 30th day after the sale, excluding the sale day, when the lender reserved the right to a deficiency judgment. Many lenders waive the deficiency to avoid that delay.

faqs.q: Do I need an attorney to close in South Carolina?
faqs.a: Yes. South Carolina requires a licensed South Carolina attorney to supervise the real estate closing.

faqs.q: Can I sell my house during a South Carolina foreclosure?
faqs.a: Yes, until the sale is complete. Because the process is judicial, South Carolina timelines are generally longer than Georgia's, which leaves more room to close a sale.

title: What Cash Home Buyers Actually Pay, and How the Offer Gets Built
desc: The real arithmetic behind a cash offer: after-repair value minus repairs, minus holding and closing costs, minus margin. Including where the '70% rule' comes from.
answer: A cash offer is built from four numbers: the after-repair value of the house, the cost of repairs, holding and closing costs, and the buyer's margin. Offer = ARV − repairs − holding/closing − margin. Many investors shorthand this as the 70% rule (offer roughly 70% of ARV minus repairs), but that's a rule of thumb for a specific kind of deal, not a law. On a lightly-worn house in a strong market the number lands well above it; on a heavy rehab it lands below.

p: What the house sells for once it's fixed, based on recent comparable sales within a tight radius. Not Zillow's number, and not what the neighbor listed at. Actual closed sales of similar houses, adjusted for size and condition.
This is where honest buyers and dishonest ones diverge. Understating ARV is the easiest way to justify a lowball, and it's invisible unless you ask to see the comps. Ask to see the comps.
What it takes to bring the house to that comparable standard. Roof, HVAC, electrical, plumbing, foundation, then cosmetics.

Repair estimates are where offers actually vary between buyers. A buyer with their own crews prices the same work lower than one subbing everything out, which is why two legitimate offers on the same house can differ by tens of thousands.

Property taxes, insurance, utilities, and financing costs while the buyer owns it, plus closing on both ends. On a four-month rehab this is real money, commonly several thousand dollars, and it scales with how long the work takes.
The buyer is a business and takes a profit. Anyone who tells you otherwise is hiding it somewhere else in the math.

What you should expect is that the margin is disclosed rather than buried. A buyer who'll walk you through all four numbers is easier to evaluate than one who hands you a figure and calls it 'what the market supports'.

It's a screening heuristic from the fix-and-flip world: offer no more than 70% of ARV minus repairs, so the deal survives a cost overrun or a soft resale. It exists to protect the buyer, not to describe the market.
Treat a quoted 70% as a starting point to interrogate, not a ceiling you're stuck with. Condition, location, and how fast the buyer needs to deploy capital all move it.
sections.callout: The comparison that matters isn't cash offer versus list price. It's cash offer versus net proceeds from listing: sale price, minus 5–6% commission, minus 1–3% closing costs, minus repair credits after inspection, minus months of carrying costs, minus the risk the financed buyer's loan falls through. Run both columns before you decide.

list: An offer given before anyone has seen the property or asked about its condition
Refusal to show comparable sales
Large non-refundable earnest money demanded up front
Pressure to sign the same day
A contract that's assignable with no cap and no disclosure — that's a wholesaler shopping your house, not a buyer
A number that changes downward after inspection with no new information

faqs.q: How much do cash home buyers typically pay?
faqs.a: It depends entirely on condition and market, but the arithmetic is consistent: after-repair value minus repair cost minus holding and closing costs minus margin. A light-cosmetic house in a strong market gets a much higher percentage of value than a full gut rehab.

faqs.q: What is the 70% rule?
faqs.a: A fix-and-flip screening heuristic: offer no more than 70% of after-repair value minus repair costs. It exists to protect the buyer's downside, not to describe what a house is worth. Use it to sanity-check an offer, not to accept one.

faqs.q: Why do two cash offers on the same house differ so much?
faqs.a: Mostly repair estimates. A buyer with in-house crews prices the same scope well below one subcontracting everything. Differences in assumed after-repair value and required margin account for the rest.

faqs.q: Should I get more than one cash offer?
faqs.a: Yes, and any legitimate buyer will tell you the same. Ask each one to show the comps and the repair scope behind their number. The buyer who won't show their work is telling you something.

faqs.q: Is a cash offer always lower than listing?
faqs.a: On the headline number, usually. On net proceeds, not always — commission, closing costs, repair credits, and months of carrying costs come off a listing. Compare the net figures, not the asking price.

title: Selling an Inherited House: What Probate Actually Requires Before You Can Sell
desc: You can't sell an inherited house until someone has legal authority to sign the deed. Here's how probate grants it, what it costs to wait, and what heirs can do meanwhile.
answer: You can't sell an inherited house until the estate has a court-appointed personal representative — an executor named in the will or an administrator appointed when there's no will. That person signs the deed, not the heirs individually, unless the will granted an independent power of sale or the property passed outside probate through a trust, joint tenancy, or a transfer-on-death deed. Inherited property generally receives a stepped-up cost basis to fair market value at the date of death, which often means little or no capital gain if you sell soon after.

p: This is the question that determines everything else. Being an heir doesn't give you authority to convey real estate. Authority comes from the court, in the form of letters testamentary or letters of administration.

Until those letters issue, a buyer's closing attorney or title company can't insure the transfer, so a sale can't close. You can sign a contract contingent on the appointment, and you should — locking in a price while probate runs is exactly the right move.

list: The property was held in a living trust — the successor trustee can sell without probate
It was owned in joint tenancy with right of survivorship — it passes to the survivor automatically
A transfer-on-death deed was recorded (available in some states)
The estate qualifies for a small estate procedure, though these usually cover personal property rather than real estate

p: The estate keeps paying while probate runs, and the bills don't pause for grief.

Property taxes continue. Insurance gets expensive or gets cancelled once the carrier learns the house is vacant — most standard policies restrict coverage after 30 to 60 days of vacancy. Utilities have to stay on enough to prevent frozen pipes and mold. Someone has to cut the grass or the county starts issuing citations.
sections.callout: The single most common expensive mistake with an inherited house is letting the homeowners policy lapse. Call the carrier, tell them the house is vacant, and get a vacant-property policy in place. It costs more than the old policy and far less than an uninsured loss.

p: Every heir with an ownership interest generally has to sign unless the will gave the executor independent power of sale. That's where inherited-house sales stall for years.
A firm written offer often breaks the deadlock, because it converts an argument about a hypothetical listing price into a decision about one real number everyone can divide.

Across the Southeast, and especially in coastal Georgia and South Carolina, a great deal of land is held as heirs' property: it passed down for generations without probate or recorded deeds, so ownership is now split among dozens of descendants, many unaware they own anything.

Selling requires either every owner signing or a court process, and it takes months rather than weeks. If this describes your situation, start with a real estate attorney who handles heirs' property specifically. It's solvable, but not quickly.

Inherited property generally gets a stepped-up basis to fair market value on the date of death. Sell near that value and there's often little or no capital gain. Sell years later after appreciation and there may be.
None of that is tax advice, and the details vary with the estate. Talk to a CPA before you close, not after.

faqs.q: Can I sell an inherited house before probate is complete?
faqs.a: You can sign a contract, but you generally can't close until the court has appointed a personal representative with authority to sign the deed. Getting an offer in hand while probate runs is the efficient path.

faqs.q: What if the other heirs won't agree to sell?
faqs.a: Every heir with an ownership interest generally has to sign, unless the will granted the executor an independent power of sale. If agreement is impossible, a partition action is the legal remedy, but it's slow and expensive. A concrete written offer resolves most of these disputes faster than a lawyer can.

faqs.q: Do I have to clean out the house first?
faqs.a: Not if you're selling to a cash buyer. Take what matters to you and leave everything else. Cleanout is one of the largest hidden costs of a conventional inherited-property sale.

faqs.q: Will I owe capital gains tax on an inherited house?
faqs.a: Often little or none, because inherited property generally receives a stepped-up cost basis to fair market value as of the date of death. Confirm with a CPA — this depends on the estate's specifics.

faqs.q: What is heirs' property?
faqs.a: Real estate passed down without probate or recorded deeds, so ownership fragments across many descendants over generations. It's common across the Southeast. Selling requires all owners to sign or a court process, and it takes months.

title: Cash Buyer vs. Listing With an Agent vs. iBuyer: The Honest Comparison
desc: Three ways to sell, three different tradeoffs. What each actually nets you, how long each takes, and which situations each one genuinely fits.
answer: Listing with an agent gets the highest price if your house is in good condition, you can wait 30–60 days past an accepted offer, and you can keep it showable. A cash buyer gets you a certain date and takes the house as-is, at a discount to retail, with no commission or closing costs. An iBuyer sits in between: near-retail offers on newer, cookie-cutter homes in metro markets, but with service fees typically around 5% plus deducted repair estimates, and strict eligibility. Most distressed or older Southeastern housing stock doesn't qualify for an iBuyer at all.

p: Highest gross price. It's also the slowest and the least certain, and the costs are easy to underestimate.
list: Commission: commonly 5–6% of sale price
Seller closing costs: commonly 1–3%
Repairs and credits: negotiated after the buyer's inspection, and often required by the buyer's lender
Time: days on market, then commonly 30–60 days to close a financed offer
Risk: financed deals fail on appraisal, inspection, or loan denial
sections.callout: Best when: the house shows well, you're not on a deadline, and you can afford to carry it while it sits.

p: Lowest gross price, highest certainty. No financing contingency and no appraisal means the deal doesn't collapse three weeks in.
list: Commission: none
Closing costs: typically paid by the buyer
Repairs: none — the discount is the repair budget
Time: 7–28 days
Risk: low, provided the buyer is the actual buyer and not a wholesaler shopping your contract
sections.callout: Best when: the house needs work, it's occupied or vacant and costing you money, there's a deadline (foreclosure, probate, relocation), or you simply don't want to manage a sale.

p: Algorithmic offers on homes that fit a narrow profile: relatively new, standard layout, in a metro area with enough comparable volume to model.

The offer looks close to retail until you read the deductions. Service fees typically run around 5%, and the platform deducts its own repair estimate after inspection — an estimate you have limited ability to contest.
list: Service fee: commonly around 5%
Repair deductions: assessed after their inspection
Eligibility: restrictive on age, condition, and location
Time: typically a few weeks
sections.callout: Best when: your house is newer, in good shape, in a large metro, and you want speed without negotiating. Most of the housing stock in Waycross, Selma, or rural Bulloch County isn't eligible.

p: Take the listing price you'd realistically get. Subtract 6% commission. Subtract 2% closing costs. Subtract what an inspector will find. Subtract your mortgage payment, taxes, insurance, and utilities for the months it takes.

Compare that figure to the cash offer. Sometimes listing still wins by a wide margin, and when it does, take it. Sometimes the gap is a few thousand dollars and four months of stress, and that's a genuinely different decision.

faqs.q: Which nets the most money?
faqs.a: Usually listing with an agent, if the house is in good condition and you can wait. Once you subtract commission, closing costs, repair credits, and carrying costs, the gap narrows more than most sellers expect — and on a house needing significant work it can close entirely.

faqs.q: Are iBuyer offers really close to market value?
faqs.a: The headline offer often is. The net is lower after a service fee of roughly 5% and repair deductions assessed following their inspection. Eligibility is also restrictive, so many older Southeastern homes don't qualify.

faqs.q: How do I know if a cash buyer is legitimate?
faqs.a: Ask whether they're the actual buyer or assigning the contract. Ask to see proof of funds. Ask to see the comparable sales behind their number. Check that the entity name on the contract matches a real registered company. A real buyer answers all four without hesitating.

faqs.q: Can I list first and sell to a cash buyer if it doesn't work?
faqs.a: Yes, and plenty of people do. Just check your listing agreement for the protection period clause, which can obligate commission on a sale to a buyer the agent introduced, and understand when your listing term expires.

faqs.q: What's the fastest option?
faqs.a: A cash buyer. Seven to 28 days is normal, versus a few weeks for an iBuyer and 30–60 days after an accepted offer on a financed listing.

title: Selling a House With Liens: What Gets Paid, What Gets Negotiated, What Stops a Sale
desc: Mortgages, judgments, tax liens, HOA balances, mechanic's liens. Which ones come off at closing, which need negotiating, and which actually block a transfer.
answer: Most liens don't stop a sale — they get paid at closing out of the proceeds. The closing attorney or title company runs a title search, identifies every recorded encumbrance, pays them from the sale, and issues clear title. You need no cash up front. The liens that genuinely block a sale are the ones nobody can locate a payoff for: a mortgage never released after payoff, a judgment against someone with a similar name, or a deed that was never updated after a death.

sections.h: The ones that just get paid
list: Mortgages and HELOCs. Payoff is ordered from the servicer and wired at closing.
Property tax liens. The county gives a payoff good through a date. Paid from proceeds.
HOA assessments. The association issues an estoppel or payoff letter. Paid at closing.
Judgment liens. A recorded judgment attaches to real property in the county where it's recorded. It's paid or negotiated down at closing.
Mechanic's / materialman's liens. A contractor who wasn't paid can record one. Paid, bonded around, or negotiated.

sections.h: The ones that need real work
p: An unreleased mortgage. You paid the loan off in 2009, but the lender never recorded a satisfaction, and now the lender doesn't exist. Curing this means tracking the successor institution or filing a quiet title action.
IRS liens. A federal tax lien can often be paid or discharged at closing, but the IRS has a formal process with its own timeline. Start early.

A dead co-owner still on the deed. Very common. The deed says you and your late spouse or parent. Until the estate is handled or an heirship affidavit is recorded, you can't convey the whole interest.
Heirs' property. Ownership fragmented across a generation with no probate. Months, not weeks.
sections.callout: None of these are unusual, and none of them are the end of a sale. What they all share is that they take time to cure — which is exactly why a financed retail buyer, locked into a 30-day rate lock, walks away when one surfaces. A cash buyer with no lender clock can wait it out.

sections.h: What if the liens exceed the value
p: Then the deal depends on negotiation. Judgment creditors frequently accept less than face value for a certain payment now. Counties will sometimes reduce accumulated code-enforcement fines when a buyer commits to fixing the underlying violation. HOAs negotiate.
If the mortgage alone exceeds value, that's a short sale, and it needs the lender's approval — generally 45 to 90 days depending on the servicer.
Before you assume the worst, get a title search. A closing attorney or title company can run one for a modest fee, and plenty of buyers will order one at their own cost early in the process.

Sellers are frequently wrong about what's recorded against their property, in both directions. People discover liens they'd never heard of, and just as often discover a lien they've been worrying about was released years ago.

faqs.q: Can I sell a house that has a lien on it?
faqs.a: Yes. Most liens are paid at closing out of the sale proceeds, the same way a mortgage payoff is. You don't need to clear them beforehand or bring cash to the table.

faqs.q: What if the liens are more than the house is worth?
faqs.a: Then it becomes a negotiation. Judgment creditors often accept a reduced payoff, and counties will sometimes reduce code-enforcement fines for a buyer who commits to fixing the problem. If the mortgage alone exceeds value, that's a short sale requiring lender approval.

faqs.q: Who finds the liens?
faqs.a: The closing attorney or title company runs a title search and identifies every recorded encumbrance. That search is what makes clear title possible, and it's why you can't skip the closing professional.

faqs.q: What's the hardest lien problem to fix?
faqs.a: Usually a title defect rather than a lien: an unreleased mortgage from a lender that no longer exists, or a deceased co-owner never removed from the deed. Both need legal work, and both take months rather than days.

faqs.q: Does a lien have to be paid before I can sign a contract?
faqs.a: No. You can sign a purchase contract with liens outstanding. They're resolved during the title process and satisfied at closing.

title: Selling a Rental Property With Tenants Still in It
desc: Leases survive a sale. Here's what transfers, what notice you owe, what happens to the security deposit, and why you don't need to evict before selling.
answer: You can sell a rental with tenants in place, and you don't have to evict first. A lease is attached to the property, not the owner, so it survives the sale and the buyer becomes the new landlord on the existing terms. The security deposit transfers to the buyer at closing, normally as a credit on the settlement statement. What makes tenant-occupied properties hard to sell conventionally isn't the law — it's that retail buyers want vacant possession and their lenders scrutinize condition.

list: The lease, on its existing terms, including the rent amount and the end date
The security deposit, credited to the buyer at closing so they carry the obligation to return it
Any prepaid rent, prorated at closing
Pending repair obligations under the lease

p: A fixed-term lease runs to its end date regardless of who owns the building. A buyer who wants the unit vacant has to wait it out or negotiate with the tenant.
A month-to-month tenancy can be terminated with proper statutory notice, which varies by state. That flexibility makes month-to-month properties easier to sell to owner-occupants.
Showings require tenant cooperation and legal notice, and a tenant who doesn't want to move has no incentive to keep the place presentable. Photos get taken around clutter. Access gets refused.

Then there's financing. An FHA or VA buyer generally has to occupy the property, which a lease prevents. Conventional investor financing has its own condition requirements, and a deferred-maintenance rental often fails them.
sections.callout: This is why tenant-occupied properties sell at a discount on the open market even when they're in decent shape. The buyer pool shrinks to cash and to investors with flexible financing, and both price accordingly.

p: A tenant who's stopped paying doesn't kill a sale to a cash buyer. It reduces what the property is worth, because the buyer absorbs the cost and delay of resolving it, but it's a price adjustment rather than a disqualification.

Selling occupied is frequently better arithmetic than evicting first. An eviction costs filing fees, attorney time, and one to three months of continued non-payment, and then you still have to sell a vacant property that may have been damaged on the way out.

State law and your lease govern the specifics, but generally you must notify the tenant of the ownership change and tell them where to send rent. Handle the security deposit correctly at closing so you're clean on your obligation to return it.
Give the tenant honest notice. A tenant who finds out from a stranger at the door is a tenant who stops paying and calls a legal aid office.

faqs.q: Can I sell my rental property with tenants still living there?
faqs.a: Yes. The lease transfers with the property and the buyer becomes the landlord on the existing terms. No eviction is needed, and a cash buyer doesn't need showings.

faqs.q: What happens to the security deposit when I sell?
faqs.a: It transfers to the buyer at closing, usually as a credit on the settlement statement. That makes the buyer responsible for returning it and keeps you clean on the obligation.

faqs.q: Do I have to tell my tenant I'm selling?
faqs.a: State law and your lease govern the specifics, but you generally must notify the tenant of the ownership change and where to send rent going forward. Telling them early avoids most problems.

faqs.q: What if my tenant hasn't paid rent in months?
faqs.a: It affects the price, not whether a cash buyer will purchase. Selling occupied is often better math than evicting first, since eviction costs filing fees, attorney time, and additional months of non-payment before you can even list.

faqs.q: Does the buyer have to honor the existing lease?
faqs.a: Yes. A fixed-term lease runs to its end date regardless of ownership change. A month-to-month tenancy can be terminated with proper statutory notice.

title: What Selling a House 'As-Is' Actually Means (and What It Doesn't)
desc: As-is means you make no repairs. It does not mean you can hide known defects. Here's the difference, and what disclosure still applies in the Southeast.
answer: Selling as-is means you make no repairs and offer no repair credits — the buyer takes the property in its current condition. It does not mean you can conceal known material defects. Disclosure obligations survive an as-is sale in every state, and actively hiding a known problem is fraud regardless of contract language. As-is protects you from being nickel-and-dimed after an inspection. It doesn't protect you from lying.

list: No repairs before closing, and no repair credits negotiated after inspection
No repainting, re-carpeting, or cosmetic prep
No requirement to bring anything up to current code
No cleanout — with a cash buyer, contents can stay

p: It doesn't erase disclosure. If you know the basement floods, that the roof leaks into the back bedroom, or that there was a meth lab in the garage, you generally have to say so.

Southeastern states vary on how formal that duty is. Some require a standardized written disclosure form; others follow a modified caveat emptor rule where the duty attaches to latent defects the buyer couldn't reasonably discover. In every one of them, active concealment is actionable.
sections.callout: The practical rule is simple and it protects you: disclose everything you know, in writing. A buyer who's told about the foundation crack and buys anyway has no claim. A buyer who discovers it after closing and can show you knew has a very good one.

p: As-is doesn't mean no inspection. Most as-is contracts still give the buyer an inspection period, and a buyer who finds something they didn't expect can typically terminate.

The difference is what happens next. In a standard contract the buyer comes back asking for repairs or credits. In an as-is contract they either proceed or walk. That's a meaningful reduction in the number of ways your sale can fall apart.

sections.h: As-is and financing don't mix well
p: This is what sends most as-is sellers to a cash buyer. FHA and VA appraisers flag health and safety issues — active leaks, exposed wiring, missing handrails, a roof with under two years of life. When they do, the lender makes the loan conditional on repairs.
Which means that in practice, an as-is sale to a financed buyer often isn't as-is at all. You end up paying for repairs before closing, on a house you'd agreed to sell in current condition.

faqs.q: Does selling as-is mean I don't have to disclose problems?
faqs.a: No. As-is governs repairs, not disclosure. You still have to disclose known material defects, and actively concealing one is fraud regardless of what the contract says.

faqs.q: Can a buyer still inspect an as-is house?
faqs.a: Usually yes. Most as-is contracts include an inspection period. The difference is the buyer's remedy: they proceed or terminate, rather than coming back to negotiate repairs and credits.

faqs.q: Will a lender finance an as-is house?
faqs.a: Sometimes, but FHA and VA appraisers flag health and safety issues and lenders then require repairs before funding. That's why as-is sales to financed buyers frequently stop being as-is in practice.

faqs.q: Do I need a written disclosure form?
faqs.a: It depends on the state. Some require a standardized form; others apply a modified caveat emptor rule covering latent defects. Disclosing in writing is the safe practice everywhere.

faqs.q: Does as-is lower my price?
faqs.a: It typically lowers the gross price, because the buyer is absorbing the repair cost and the risk. What you save is the repair spend, the credits, and the months of carrying costs while the work gets done.

title: Property Tax Sales in the Southeast: How Long You Really Have
desc: Delinquent property taxes lead to a tax sale, and the rules differ sharply by state. Redemption periods, what you can still do, and how they differ from foreclosure.
answer: A property tax sale is not the same thing as a mortgage foreclosure, and the timelines are completely different. Georgia gives a 12-month redemption after a tax sale. South Carolina also allows 12 months. Alabama runs a three-year administrative redemption. Florida sells tax certificates first, and you can redeem any time before a tax deed is sold. North Carolina forecloses tax liens through the courts, with payoff possible until the sale is confirmed. Delinquent taxes are a lien — they get paid at closing from proceeds, so you can sell without cash up front.

p: A mortgage foreclosure comes from your lender. A tax sale comes from the county. They run on different statutes, different timelines, and different notice requirements, and a property can be in both at once.
The confusion costs people. A Georgia homeowner who hears 'twelve month redemption' and relaxes may be thinking of the tax sale rule while facing a mortgage foreclosure with no redemption at all.

list: Georgia: 12-month redemption running from the sale date. You reimburse the purchaser what they paid plus statutory premium.
South Carolina: 12-month redemption after a delinquent tax sale, run by the county Delinquent Tax Collector.
Alabama: three-year administrative redemption, with additional judicial redemption rights in some cases.

Florida: counties sell tax certificates to investors. The certificate holder can apply for a tax deed sale after a statutory period. You can redeem by paying the certificate plus interest any time before that deed sale.
North Carolina: counties foreclose tax liens through the courts rather than selling certificates. You can pay off taxes and costs until the court confirms the sale.
Tennessee: tax sales run through chancery court by the county trustee, with a redemption period after confirmation, commonly one year and shortened for longer-delinquent property.

sections.h: Why redemption is harder than it sounds
p: Redeeming means paying the purchaser everything they put in — the bid, statutory interest or premium, taxes they've paid since, and in some states the cost of improvements. It's a lump sum, and it grows.
Owners who couldn't pay a $6,000 tax bill rarely find $11,000 a year later. The redemption right is real, but it's a legal backstop rather than a practical plan.
sections.callout: If you can't pay the taxes, selling before the tax sale is almost always better than counting on redemption. The lien comes off at closing from proceeds and you keep the remaining equity, instead of watching it get consumed by penalties and premiums.

sections.h: You can sell with taxes owed
p: This is the part sellers most often don't know. Delinquent property taxes are a lien on the property, and liens are paid at closing out of sale proceeds — exactly like a mortgage.
You don't need to clear them first. You don't need cash. The county gives a payoff good through a specific date, the closing professional pays it, and the balance goes to you.

faqs.q: Can I sell a house with unpaid property taxes?
faqs.a: Yes. Delinquent taxes are a lien and get paid at closing out of the sale proceeds, exactly like a mortgage payoff. You don't need to pay them first or bring cash to closing.

faqs.q: How long do I have to redeem after a Georgia tax sale?
faqs.a: Twelve months from the sale date. You'd reimburse the purchaser what they paid plus the statutory premium. Note this is the tax sale rule — Georgia mortgage foreclosures carry no redemption at all.

faqs.q: Is a tax sale the same as foreclosure?
faqs.a: No. A tax sale is initiated by the county for unpaid property taxes. A foreclosure is initiated by your lender for unpaid mortgage debt. Different statutes, different timelines, and a property can face both simultaneously.

faqs.q: How does Florida's tax certificate system work?
faqs.a: Counties sell tax certificates to investors who pay the delinquent taxes and earn interest. After a statutory period, the certificate holder can apply for a tax deed sale. You can redeem by paying the certificate plus interest any time before that deed sale happens.

faqs.q: What's the redemption period in Alabama?
faqs.a: Alabama allows a three-year administrative redemption period after a tax sale, with additional judicial redemption rights available in some circumstances. It's the longest window among the states covered here.

title: Selling the House During a Divorce Without Making It Worse
desc: Who has to sign, how proceeds get split, what a court order changes, and why a cash sale often ends the fight faster than a listing does.
answer: If both spouses are on the deed, both generally have to sign — unless a divorce decree or court order directs the sale, in which case that order controls. Proceeds are disbursed by the closing attorney or title company according to the order or your written joint instructions, usually as two separate payments rather than one spouse handling the other's money. A cash sale removes the parts of a listing that generate the most conflict: pricing, agent selection, repairs, staging, and which offer to accept.

p: Title controls. If the deed names both spouses, both signatures are needed to convey. If only one name is on the deed, marital property rules in your state may still give the other spouse rights that have to be released at closing.
A court order directing sale substitutes for a reluctant spouse's cooperation. If you're stuck, that's what your attorney is for.
The closing professional disburses according to written joint instructions or the court order. Two wires, two checks — not one lump sum to one spouse who then owes the other.
Say this explicitly in the contract and in the closing instructions. It's the single easiest way to prevent a post-closing dispute.
sections.callout: Get the split in writing before closing, signed by both parties or ordered by the court. Closing attorneys and title companies will not guess, and an unresolved instruction will stop a disbursement on the day of closing.

sections.h: Why a listing multiplies the fights
p: Every step of a conventional sale is a decision two people who are divorcing have to agree on. What price. Which agent. Whether to accept $8,000 under asking. Whether to do the $4,000 of repairs the inspector flagged. Whether to drop the price after 45 days.
And through all of it, someone has to keep the house showable, which usually means the spouse still living there is doing unpaid work to benefit both.
One number, one date, no repairs, no showings, no staging. There's a single decision to make instead of a dozen.
It also lets each side stop coordinating with the other. We've closed transactions where the two spouses never sat in the same room, signing separately with their own attorneys.

Often one spouse is still living in the house and needs somewhere to go. A post-closing occupancy agreement handles this: the sale closes, the money is disbursed, and the occupying spouse has a defined period to move.
Put it in the contract. Handshake arrangements between divorcing spouses about move-out dates are exactly the kind of thing that ends up back in front of a judge.

faqs.q: Do both spouses have to agree to sell the house?
faqs.a: If both are on the deed, generally yes — unless a divorce decree or court order directs the sale, which substitutes for the reluctant spouse's cooperation. Your divorce attorney can tell you exactly where you stand.

faqs.q: How do the sale proceeds get divided?
faqs.a: The closing attorney or title company disburses according to the court order or written joint instructions from both parties, typically as two separate payments. Get that instruction in writing before closing day.

faqs.q: What if one spouse refuses to sign?
faqs.a: That's what a court order is for. Once a judge directs the sale, the order can substitute for the missing signature or authorize someone to sign on that spouse's behalf.

faqs.q: Can one spouse stay in the house after closing?
faqs.a: Yes, with a written post-closing occupancy agreement built into the contract. Don't rely on an informal arrangement.

faqs.q: Is a cash sale better during a divorce?
faqs.a: Often, because it collapses a dozen joint decisions into one. It typically nets less than a well-executed listing, so the tradeoff is money against speed and reduced conflict. If both parties can cooperate on a listing, that usually pays more.

title: The Vacant House Problem: Why Your Insurance May Already Have Lapsed
desc: Most homeowners policies restrict coverage after 30 to 60 days of vacancy. If you own an empty house, this is the most expensive thing you don't know.
answer: Most standard homeowners policies restrict or void coverage once a house has been vacant beyond 30 to 60 days. Owners of inherited, rental, or relocation-stranded houses routinely discover this only after a loss, when the claim is denied. Replacing it with a vacant-property policy typically costs considerably more for less coverage. Combined with deterioration, code enforcement, and theft risk, a vacant house is the most expensive kind of property to own and do nothing about.

p: Pull your policy and look for a vacancy or unoccupancy provision. The typical language suspends coverage for vandalism, glass breakage, water damage, and sometimes theft after a defined vacancy period, commonly 30 or 60 consecutive days.
The distinction between vacant and unoccupied matters too. A furnished house between tenants may be unoccupied but not vacant. An empty house with the utilities off is vacant.
sections.callout: If you own an empty house right now, stop and call your carrier before you finish this page. A vacant-property policy costs more than your old one and vastly less than an uninsured total loss.

sections.h: What actually goes wrong in an empty house
list: Water. A supply line lets go and runs for weeks. This is the single most common catastrophic vacant-house loss.
Mold. In the Southeast's humidity, an unconditioned house grows mold within weeks, not months.
Roof failure. A leak nobody sees rots decking and then framing.
Copper theft. Thieves strip plumbing and HVAC line sets, which then floods the house.
Squatters. Removing them means an eviction-style legal process, not a call to police.
Code enforcement. Tall grass and visible deterioration generate citations, then daily fines, then liens.

sections.h: The carrying cost nobody adds up
p: Property taxes. Insurance, now at vacant-property rates. Utilities you have to keep on to prevent freezing and mold. Lawn service so the county doesn't cite you. HOA dues. And the mortgage, if there is one.

Across the Southeast that commonly runs several hundred to well over a thousand dollars a month for a house producing nothing. Over the two years an inherited property often sits while heirs decide, it's a serious number.

sections.h: Selling a vacant house is usually the fastest close
p: No occupant to coordinate around, no lease to honor, no showings to schedule. Utilities don't need to be on for a cash buyer to make an offer or to close.
If you're waiting on probate, get the offer now and hold it. The clock on the insurance and the deterioration is running whether the court is or not.

faqs.q: Does homeowners insurance cover a vacant house?
faqs.a: Usually not after a defined vacancy period, commonly 30 to 60 consecutive days. Standard policies suspend coverage for vandalism, water damage, glass breakage, and sometimes theft once that period passes.

faqs.q: What is a vacant property policy?
faqs.a: A specialty policy written for unoccupied homes. It costs considerably more than standard homeowners coverage and typically covers less, but it's far better than an uninsured loss.

faqs.q: How fast can you buy a vacant house?
faqs.a: As little as 7 days from accepted offer when title is clear. Vacant properties are often the fastest closings because there's no occupant to coordinate around.

faqs.q: Do the utilities need to be on to sell?
faqs.a: No. A cash buyer can make an offer and close without power or water. A financed buyer's appraiser generally does need them on.

faqs.q: What's the biggest risk in an empty house?
faqs.a: Water. A failed supply line running unnoticed for weeks causes more catastrophic vacant-house losses than anything else, and it's frequently the loss the vacancy clause excludes.

title: How to Tell a Real Cash Buyer From a Wholesaler Shopping Your Contract
desc: Four questions that separate an actual buyer from someone assigning your contract to a stranger — plus the contract clauses worth reading before you sign.
answer: Ask four questions: Are you the buyer or are you assigning this contract? Can I see proof of funds? Can I see the comparable sales behind your number? What entity will appear on the contract? A real buyer answers all four without hesitating. Wholesaling — putting a house under contract and selling the contract to another investor — is legal in most circumstances and sometimes discloses itself clearly. The problem is the version that doesn't tell you, ties up your property, and then renegotiates when the assignment doesn't sell.

list: Are you the end buyer, or will you assign this contract? Both answers can be fine. A refusal to answer is not.
Can I see proof of funds? A bank statement or a lender letter dated recently. Not a screenshot with the numbers cropped.
Can I see your comps? The recent comparable sales the offer is built on. A buyer confident in their number shows their work.
What entity goes on the contract? Then look it up in the state's business registry. The name should match a real, active company.

sections.h: Contract clauses to read before signing
p: The assignment clause. Language allowing assignment 'to any party' with no notice means your contract can be sold. If they've told you they're the buyer, that clause contradicts them.
Inspection or due diligence period. A long one — 21 or 30 days — with unilateral termination lets a wholesaler tie up your property while shopping it, then walk with no consequence.
Earnest money. A hundred dollars of refundable earnest money on a $200,000 house is not commitment. It's an option.
Memorandum of contract. A clause allowing them to record a memorandum against your title clouds it, and can make selling to anyone else difficult until they release it.
sections.callout: The single most useful protection: meaningful, non-refundable-after-inspection earnest money held by a closing attorney or title company. A buyer who intends to close will post it. One who's shopping your contract will find reasons not to.

list: An offer given before anyone asked about the property's condition
Pressure to sign today, or an offer that 'expires' in hours
Refusal to put the offer in writing
A price that drops after inspection with no new information
Being asked to sign a deed rather than a purchase contract
Requests for money up front for any reason
No verifiable business address or registration

p: A real buyer explains the four numbers behind the offer, puts it in writing with no obligation, uses a licensed closing attorney or title company, posts real earnest money, and tells you when listing with an agent would net you more.
That last one is the strongest signal there is. A buyer willing to talk themselves out of a deal is a buyer telling you the truth about the ones they do take.

faqs.q: Is wholesaling real estate legal?
faqs.a: In most circumstances yes, though several states have added licensing or disclosure requirements. The issue isn't legality — it's disclosure. A wholesaler who tells you what they're doing is doing business. One who claims to be the buyer while shopping your contract is not.

faqs.q: How do I know if a cash buyer is legitimate?
faqs.a: Ask whether they're the end buyer or assigning, ask for recent proof of funds, ask to see the comparable sales behind the offer, and verify the entity name on the contract in the state business registry. Real buyers answer all four easily.

faqs.q: What is an assignment clause?
faqs.a: Contract language letting the buyer transfer their rights to someone else. Broad assignment language with no notice requirement means your contract can be sold to a stranger who may want different terms.

faqs.q: How much earnest money should a cash buyer put up?
faqs.a: Enough to represent real commitment, held by a closing attorney or title company. A token amount that's fully refundable through a long due diligence period functions as a free option on your house, not a purchase.

faqs.q: Should I ever sign a deed instead of a purchase contract?
faqs.a: No. A purchase contract obligates a sale on defined terms with a closing. A deed transfers ownership immediately. If someone asks you to sign a deed outside a closing, stop and call an attorney.

title: Closing Costs in the Southeast: Who Pays What, and What a Cash Sale Removes
desc: Attorney states, title states, transfer taxes, prorations. What a seller normally pays across GA, SC, FL, AL, NC and TN — and which of those a cash sale eliminates.
answer: Sellers typically pay 1–3% of the sale price in closing costs on top of a 5–6% agent commission. Georgia, South Carolina, and North Carolina are attorney closing states — a licensed attorney must handle the closing. Florida, Alabama, and Tennessee typically use title companies. In a cash sale to a buyer who pays closing costs, the seller's side generally reduces to the payoffs and prorations attached to the property itself.

p: Attorney required: Georgia, South Carolina, North Carolina. A licensed attorney in that state supervises the closing, runs title, and handles disbursement.
Title company typical: Florida, Alabama, Tennessee. A title company or closing agent handles it; an attorney isn't required.

This affects your timeline more than your cost. An attorney's calendar is a scheduling constraint that a title company's usually isn't, which matters when you're closing against a foreclosure sale date.

sections.h: What a seller normally pays on a listed sale
list: Agent commission: commonly 5–6%, the largest single line
Transfer tax or deed stamps: varies by state and county
Attorney or closing fee: where the seller's side bears one
Owner's title policy: customary for the seller in some markets, the buyer in others
Prorated property taxes through the closing date
Repair credits negotiated after inspection
Payoffs: mortgage, HELOC, liens, HOA balances, delinquent taxes

sections.h: What comes off in a cash sale
p: Commission goes to zero — there's no listing agent and no buyer's agent. Closing costs, in a deal where the buyer covers them, go to zero on your side. Repair credits go to zero because there are no repairs.
What doesn't go away: the payoffs and prorations. Your mortgage, liens, back taxes, and HOA balance are debts attached to the property. They're satisfied at closing regardless of who buys it.
sections.callout: The clearest way to compare offers is the net sheet — the settlement statement figure showing what actually reaches you. Ask every buyer and every agent for one. A gross price is not a comparison.

p: Property taxes are divided at closing based on the date. You pay for the portion of the year you owned it; the buyer pays the rest. The same applies to HOA dues and, on a rental, to rent and the security deposit.
These appear as credits and debits on the settlement statement and typically move the final number by a few hundred to a few thousand dollars.

faqs.q: How much are seller closing costs?
faqs.a: Typically 1–3% of the sale price, on top of a 5–6% agent commission on a listed sale. In a cash sale where the buyer pays closing costs, the seller's side generally reduces to the payoffs and prorations attached to the property.

faqs.q: Which Southeastern states require an attorney at closing?
faqs.a: Georgia, South Carolina, and North Carolina require a licensed attorney to handle the closing. Florida, Alabama, and Tennessee typically use title companies instead.

faqs.q: What is a net sheet?
faqs.a: A breakdown showing what actually reaches you after commission, closing costs, payoffs, and prorations. It's the only fair way to compare a cash offer against a listing, since gross prices aren't comparable.

faqs.q: Do I pay property taxes for the whole year if I sell mid-year?
faqs.a: No. Taxes are prorated at closing so you pay only for the portion of the year you owned the property. The proration appears on the settlement statement.

faqs.q: Who pays for the title search?
faqs.a: It varies by state and by local custom, and it's negotiable. In a cash purchase where the buyer covers closing costs, the buyer generally pays for the search and the title policy.

title: Do You Need a Realtor to Sell Your House? An Honest Answer
desc: No, you don't legally need one. Here's when an agent clearly earns their commission, when they clearly don't, and how to tell which situation you're in.
answer: No state requires you to use a real estate agent to sell your own house. Whether you should is a different question. An agent earns their commission when the house shows well, the market is competitive, and exposure drives multiple offers — the price lift routinely exceeds the fee. An agent adds less when the house needs significant work, when the buyer pool is investors rather than owner-occupants, or when you have a hard deadline a 30-to-60-day financed closing can't meet.

sections.h: When an agent is clearly worth it
p: A house in good condition, in a neighborhood with active demand, priced right, exposed to the full MLS buyer pool. Competition between financed buyers is what produces above-asking offers, and you don't get that selling privately to one person.
Agents also manage the parts that go wrong: the appraisal that comes in low, the inspection negotiation, the lender that goes quiet at day 25. That's real work and it has real value.

list: The house needs work that financed buyers' lenders won't approve
You have a deadline shorter than a financed closing takes
The house is occupied by a tenant who won't cooperate with showings
The realistic buyer pool is investors, who don't need an agent to find you
You're selling to a specific known buyer already

p: If you sign a listing agreement, read the protection or protection period clause. It typically obligates you to pay commission if you sell to a buyer the agent introduced, for a defined period after the listing expires.
This catches people who list, don't sell, let the listing lapse, and then sell to someone who toured during the listing. Know the term before you sign.
sections.callout: If you're considering both a listing and a cash sale, get the cash offer before you sign a listing agreement. Once you're under a listing, a subsequent sale may trigger commission depending on the agreement's terms.

p: It's legal everywhere and it isn't complicated when the buyer is experienced. You'll still use a closing attorney or title company, which is where the actual legal work happens.
What you take on yourself: pricing, disclosure, negotiating, and coordinating the closing. What you save: the listing side of the commission, commonly 2.5–3%.

Tossie Griner holds real estate licenses in Georgia and South Carolina. When we buy your house we're not acting as your agent — we're the buyer, and we represent ourselves. That's disclosed on every page of this site because it should be.
You're welcome to have your own agent or attorney review anything we send you. Plenty of our sellers do, and none of them have regretted it.

faqs.q: Do I legally need a realtor to sell my house?
faqs.a: No. No state requires a seller to use a real estate agent. You will typically need a closing attorney or title company, depending on the state, since that's where the legal transfer happens.

faqs.q: How much commission do I save selling without an agent?
faqs.a: Selling directly to a buyer with no agents involved saves the full commission, commonly 5–6%. Selling without a listing agent but to an agent-represented buyer typically saves the listing side, around 2.5–3%.

faqs.q: What is a protection period in a listing agreement?
faqs.a: A clause obligating you to pay commission if you sell to a buyer the agent introduced, for a defined period after the listing expires. Read the term before signing, especially if you're also considering a cash offer.

faqs.q: When is listing with an agent clearly better?
faqs.a: When the house is in good condition, you can wait 30–60 days past an accepted offer, and you can keep it showable. Competition between financed buyers usually produces a price lift that exceeds the commission.

faqs.q: Is a licensed agent buying my house a conflict of interest?
faqs.a: It's why disclosure matters. When a licensee buys for their own account they're a principal, not your agent, and they owe you no agency duties. That should be stated plainly in writing, and you should feel free to get your own representation.

title: Selling a Fire Damaged House: Insurance, Smoke, and Why Financing Disappears
desc: Fire damage isn't just what burned. Smoke, water, and mold follow it, financed buyers vanish, and the insurance decision shapes everything.
answer: A fire-damaged house generally can't be sold to a financed buyer — lenders won't fund an uninhabitable structure, so the buyer pool narrows to cash investors. The damage is also broader than the burn: smoke penetrates drywall and framing well beyond the fire's footprint, and the water used to extinguish it causes its own damage and then mold, often within days in Southeastern humidity. The key decision is whether you keep the insurance proceeds and sell the structure, or fold the claim into the sale.

sections.h: The damage is bigger than the burn
p: Smoke travels. It permeates drywall, insulation, ductwork, and framing in rooms the fire never reached, and the odor doesn't come out without removing material. Any honest scope of work extends well past the visibly damaged area.

Then there's the water. Suppression puts thousands of gallons into a structure, and in this climate mold begins colonizing within 24 to 48 hours. A house that burned in July and sat tarped through August has a mold problem on top of a fire problem.
Lenders require the collateral to be habitable and insurable. A fire-damaged structure is neither, so conventional, FHA, and VA financing are all off the table until it's repaired and certified.
That leaves cash. Which is not a bad thing — it just means the realistic buyer pool is investors, and pricing follows investor math rather than retail comps.
Two paths, and which is better depends on your numbers.

Keep the proceeds, sell the structure. You collect the settlement and separately sell the damaged house. Total recovery is often higher, but check whether your mortgage lender is a payee on the claim check — if so, they control the funds and typically release them against completed repairs.
Fold the claim into the sale. The buyer takes assignment of the claim as part of the price. Simpler, one transaction, and it moves the adjuster fight to someone else.
sections.callout: Don't sign your claim over to a restoration contractor before you know what the house is worth as-is. Get a cash offer first so you're comparing two real options instead of accepting the only one in front of you.

sections.h: Actual cash value vs. replacement cost
p: Check which your policy pays. Replacement cost coverage pays what it takes to rebuild. Actual cash value pays that minus depreciation, which on an older house can be dramatically less.
ACV settlements are the most common reason a fire-damaged house sits: the payout doesn't cover the rebuild, and the owner can't fund the gap.

A kitchen fire that scorched one room still contaminates the house with smoke and water damage. It's not sellable as a normal home, and buyers who tour it will smell it before they see it. Partial damage gets priced as whole-house work, because that's what remediation actually costs.

faqs.q: Can I sell a fire damaged house without repairing it?
faqs.a: Yes, to a cash buyer. Financed buyers generally can't purchase one because lenders won't fund an uninhabitable, uninsurable structure until it's repaired and certified.

faqs.q: Do I keep my insurance payout if I sell?
faqs.a: Often yes, depending on your policy and whether your mortgage lender is a payee on the check. Alternatively the buyer can take assignment of the claim as part of the price. Compare both — one usually nets more.

faqs.q: What's the difference between actual cash value and replacement cost?
faqs.a: Replacement cost pays what it takes to rebuild. Actual cash value pays that minus depreciation, which on an older roof or structure can be far less. ACV settlements are the most common reason a fire-damaged house sits unrepaired.

faqs.q: Does a small kitchen fire really affect the whole house?
faqs.a: Usually yes. Smoke permeates drywall, insulation, and ductwork well beyond the burn area, and suppression water causes secondary damage and mold. Remediation is priced as whole-house work.
